analysis.one_liner: Restores a 45 percent tax on inherited estates above $3.5 million, raising revenue from the largest inheritances.
analysis.headline: The House Democratic bill to tax estates above $3.5 million at up to 45 percent never received a hearing or a vote; Congress instead settled the estate tax at a $5.12 million exclusion and a 40 percent top rate.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have reinstated the estate tax for deaths after 2012 at a $3.5 million exemption and a top rate of 45 percent, extending the 2001 law's estate, gift, and generation-skipping tax provisions through 2013. That is a higher tax than the temporary rules then in law ($5.12 million exemption, 35 percent rate) and a lower tax than the pre-2001 rules scheduled to return ($1 million exemption, 55 percent rate). It was the Democratic leadership's fallback position in the 2012 fight over what the estate tax should be when those temporary rules expired. The bill was referred to two committees and never moved again.
analysis.who_benefits: The federal treasury and the public programs funded by general revenue, since the bill raises revenue exclusively from estates above $3.5 million — roughly the wealthiest one-third of one percent of estates. It also modestly narrows the dynastic-wealth advantage of very large inheritances compared with the rules then in effect.

how_it_helps.text: Sets a $3.5 million basic estate tax exclusion and a maximum 45 percent rate, effective for estates of decedents dying after December 31, 2012 [S2][S3].
Extends the 2001 law's estate, gift, and generation-skipping transfer tax provisions through 2013 [S2].

Includes an anti-gaming provision that claws back gift-tax benefits for gifts made while a larger exemption was in effect if the exemption falls before death, closing a loophole the 2010 law opened [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Heirs to estates worth more than $3.5 million — a small fraction of the wealthiest households — plus, in principle, some large family farms and closely held businesses that are asset-rich but cash-poor. Estate planners and wealth managers would also face clients with more tax exposure.

drawbacks.text: The bill exempts its budgetary effects from the Statutory Pay-As-You-Go Act, so the revenue it raises cannot be counted on the pay-as-you-go scorecards — a standard but transparency-weakening budget device [S2][S3].

A 45 percent rate and $3.5 million exemption would apply tax to some family farms and small businesses whose wealth is tied up in land or equipment, the concern Republicans and some farm-state Democrats raise against any estate tax revival; the bill includes no special carve-out for them [S2][S3].

Even this bill is itself a tax cut relative to pre-2001 law, which would have taxed estates above $1 million at rates up to 55 percent when the 2001 law expired at the end of 2012 — supporters accepted a higher exemption and lower rate as a negotiating compromise.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The cost falls almost entirely on the largest inheritances, which is the point of an estate tax; the main honest objections are the absence of a farm-and-small-business carve-out and the pay-as-you-go exemption. The bill was a deliberate middle ground between full repeal of the tax's revival and the pre-2001 rates, and its revenue would have been meaningful relative to the deal Congress ultimately struck.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in late July 2012 and sent to the Ways and Means and Budget Committees, and neither ever held a hearing or vote on it; the Congress ended with the bill still sitting there.

narrative.text: Representative Sander Levin introduced the bill on July 30, 2012, joined by House Democratic leaders Nancy Pelosi, Steny Hoyer, and Jim Clyburn among its 14 cosponsors [S1][S4][S5].
It was referred to the Committee on Ways and Means and to the Committee on the Budget the day it was introduced, which was the last action it ever received [S5].
The bill was written to take effect for deaths after December 31, 2012, positioning it for the end-of-2012 expiration of the temporary estate tax rules [S3].

The estate tax fight was instead settled in the January 2013 fiscal-cliff law, which set the exclusion at $5.12 million with a 40 percent top rate — a lower tax on large estates than this bill would have imposed (widely reported).

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Heirs to the largest estates came out ahead: they got the $5.12 million exemption and 40 percent rate of the January 2013 deal rather than this bill's $3.5 million and 45 percent, and the treasury collected less revenue than the bill would have raised.

for.name: Rep. Sander Levin
for.role: Ranking Democrat, House Ways and Means Committee; bill sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on July 30, 2012, as the Democratic position for the estate tax after 2012

for.name: 14 House Democrats

against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for a hearing or markup after its referral to his committee

against.name: House Republican leadership
against.what_they_did: Did not bring the bill to the floor at any point in the Congress

against.what_they_did: Set the estate tax at a $5.12 million exclusion and 40 percent rate, ending the issue on terms more favorable to large estates than this bill

sides.party_line_note: All 14 cosponsors were Democrats and no House Republican supported it; the Ways and Means chairman, a Republican, never acted on it.

industries.note: Estates above $3.5 million would have paid up to 45 percent instead of the 35 percent then in law. The bill's revenue would come from the top sliver of inheritances, and the eventual 2013 deal let those estates keep more.

industries.industry: Estate planning, trust, and wealth-management services
industries.note: A higher rate and lower exemption increase the tax stakes of large estates, driving more demand for planning designed to reduce or avoid the tax. The cost shows up as the complexity and avoidance industry that grows around any estate tax.
